---
title: "LLM-Use Statement"
description: "How LLM assistance was used to develop the MATH 346 course website and materials."
---

## Purpose Of This Statement

This page explains how large language model (LLM) assistance was used to
develop this course website and its supporting materials. It is a disclosure
about course development, not a rule governing student work.

Student use of generative AI is governed by the [Responsible AI Use
policy](syllabus/ai-policy.qmd), the [syllabus](syllabus/index.qmd), assessment
instructions, and instructor announcements. Blackboard remains authoritative
for current assessment and submission logistics.

## How LLM Assistance Was Used

This website was developed with assistance from OpenAI Codex, a coding and
writing assistant. Codex helped the instructor:

- draft, organize, and revise website pages;
- turn the course plan into weekly notes, slides, labs, exercises, and code;
- prepare project instructions, templates, synthetic-data infrastructure, and
  validation tools;
- develop assessment guides and instructor-facing implementation materials;
- check internal consistency, links, code structure, and repeated terminology;
- maintain progress records so that decisions and unfinished work remained
  visible across a long redesign process.

LLM assistance was iterative. Drafts were prompted, inspected, corrected,
rewritten, tested where possible, and sometimes rejected. The published site
should not be understood as the result of a single prompt or an autonomous
course-generation process.

## What The Instructor Determined

All course policies, assessment rules, mathematical and statistical content,
teaching priorities, project expectations, and final editorial decisions
remain the responsibility of the instructor, Laurent Alain Najman.

Important course decisions came from the instructor and the institutional
context. These include the MATLAB-to-R sequence, the emphasis on validation
and reproducibility, the assessment weights and calendar, the use of
group-specific synthetic project data, the permitted role of AI, the
requirements of Khalifa University, and revisions made in response to student
work and classroom feedback. Codex helped express and implement these choices;
it did not have authority to set them.

## Review, Testing, And Limitations

Generated suggestions were reviewed, modified, accepted, or rejected by the
instructor. Computational materials were checked with available automated
tests and manual review, and the course remains intentionally revisable when
classroom evidence identifies a problem.

LLMs can produce plausible but incorrect code, mathematics, references,
interpretations, or policy language. Automated checks also have limits. A
script that runs, a page that renders, or a numerical answer that looks
reasonable is not by itself proof that the underlying reasoning is correct.

## What This Means For Students

Students should treat the published website as instructor-authored course
material. The instructor is responsible for what is assigned and assessed,
regardless of whether an LLM assisted during preparation.

Students are encouraged to report errors, ambiguities, broken links, or
inconsistencies. If sources appear to disagree, follow the most recent
Blackboard announcement and contact the instructor. The existence of LLM
assistance in course development does not change the rules for student AI use
in a particular quiz, examination, lab, exercise, or project.
